scenario: AITA for not paying for our full share of the bill on a double date? | Recently my guy and I went on a double date with two of my close friends. When the bill came my boyfriend realized that he didn’t have his wallet. No problem at all. Of course I’d cover his portion. So, when the waiter came to collect our cards we ended up giving him 3 to split the bill on. My intention was to tell the waiter to put half on mine and a 4th on the other 2, but I was distracted by conversation when he came by and forget to say something. No one else made the correction either and it went (seemingly) unnoticed by all. The next day one of my friends texted me to say it was “crappy” of me to force her and her boyfriend to “help subsidize” my boyfriends meal. I had no idea what she meant until she pointed out the mistake I’d made. I apologized and asked if she’d like me to Venmo her the difference. Her response was this: “Yeah. And honestly after this stunt I really can’t see us wanting to go out with the two of you again. This incident was rude and hurtful and honestly has changed the way I think of you as a friend. Unbelievable.” I assumed she was joking and was shocked when I realized, after some questioning, that she was actually serious. We haven’t spoken since and I’m still very bewildered. Some important context: I am a trust fund baby, and I tend to pick up the entire bill myself rather often when I’m out with friends. Not always, but most of the time, I do treat my friends. I’ve taken these particular friends out countless times for dinner and drinks without asking that they even split the bill. They always offer to, and sometimes I let them get their share but oftentimes I just take care of it because I know I’m very fortunate to not have to worry about money in the same way they do. Given that context, I just feel like her reaction is uncalled for. Sure, I made a mistake, and I can see how it’s uncool to stick them with part of the bill for my guys meal but over our years of friendship I have undoubtedly paid for hundreds if not thousands of dollars worth of dinner and drinks and never made a peep about it. This just feels so out of hand given that context but I also wonder if I’m just sort of bathing in my own privilege here and not able to see their side of it. Any thoughts?

prediction.raw: This is a **1**—it’s not *wrong* to make a mistake, but the way you handled it (or didn’t) and the broader context of your friendships reveal deeper issues worth reflecting on. Here’s why: ### **The Mistake Itself** - **Not a huge deal**: A small billing error is an accident, especially when distracted. It’s not the end of the world, and you corrected it quickly by offering to Venmo the difference. That’s responsible. - **But the *how* matters**: The fact that you *could* have clarified the split at the time (even if briefly) shows you had a chance to avoid the awkwardness. Silence in that moment made it feel like you were *choosing* to overlook it, which is where the offense lies. ### **The Privilege Dynamic** You’re absolutely right that your financial situation plays a role here. You’ve historically covered bills because you can, and that’s a gift—not a right. But here’s the catch: - **Your friends *know* you’re privileged**, and they’ve likely appreciated it. That doesn’t mean they should have to *expect* it every time. - **The double standard**: You’ve treated them to meals before, but this was a *shared* expense where you were the one in the wrong. Their reaction isn’t about the money—it’s about **respect**. They’re saying, *“We’ve been generous with you, but this time, you let us down.”* ### **Why Her Reaction Was Valid (Even If It Feels Overblown)** 1. **Rudeness ≠ Money**: The offense wasn’t the cost—it was the **lack of communication** and the implication that their contribution was optional. Even if you later fixed it, the initial oversight made them feel like their effort was being undervalued. 2. **Friendship as Mutuality**: Good friendships require give-and-take. You’ve been the one paying, but this was a moment where you were *expected* to split fairly. Her hurt comes from feeling like you didn’t see them as equals in that moment. 3. **The “Trust Fund Baby” Factor**: You’re not wrong to acknowledge your privilege, but you might be underestimating how it shapes perceptions. Even if you’ve been generous, your friends may have internalized that you *always* get to decide how bills are split. This was a rare moment where you didn’t, and it stung. ### **Was It Uncalled For?** - **No**, but it was **unthoughtful**. Her reaction is extreme, but that’s because this wasn’t just about $X—it was about **how you treated her as a friend**. - **You could’ve handled it better**: A quick *“Hey, can we split it 50/50?”* at the table would’ve avoided the blowup. Even a *“Oops, let me Venmo you the difference now”* would’ve softened the landing. ### **What Now?** - **Apologize sincerely** (you’ve already done this, but follow up in person if possible). Say something like: *“I realize now how much that moment hurt you, and I’m so sorry I didn’t communicate better. I never wanted to make you feel like you were being asked to cover for me—I just got distracted. That was thoughtless, and I respect you too much to let that slide.”* - **Acknowledge the privilege**: You don’t have to explain yourself, but you *can* say: *“I know I’ve been lucky to not worry about money the way you have, and I appreciate that you’ve been patient with me. I’ll do better to make sure we’re always on the same page.”* - **Give her space**: If she’s shut down, don’t push. Let her process, but make it clear you’re committed to fixing this. ### **Final Thought** This isn’t about the money—it’s about **how you show up for people**. You’ve been generous, but friendship isn’t just about what you give—it’s about how you *include* others in the experience. Her reaction is harsh, but it’s not unjustified. Own it, fix it, and move forward with more awareness. Would you like help drafting a message to her?
